claims.text: High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles suppresses the driving force for phase segregation at high temperature.
High configurational entropy suppresses elemental diffusion under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
Suppression of phase segregation and elemental diffusion preserves nanoparticle structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles with intentionally reduced configurational entropy will exhibit enhanced phase segregation and degradation.
Near-equiatomic composition provides higher configurational entropy than an off-stoichiometric composition in the proposed comparison.
High configurational entropy produces homogeneous atomic mixing in solid-solution nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy increases the energy barrier for diffusion-driven segregation and phase separation.
Increasing the barrier to diffusion-driven segregation mitigates degradation at elevated temperatures.
Near-equiatomic, high-entropy nanoparticles will retain a uniform phase after high-temperature exposure.
Near-equiatomic, high-entropy nanoparticles will retain chemical uniformity after high-temperature exposure.
Off-stoichiometric, reduced-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit more phase segregation than near-equiatomic nanoparticles under identical high-temperature treatments.
Off-stoichiometric, reduced-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit more chemical heterogeneity than near-equiatomic nanoparticles under identical high-temperature treatments.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to multi-element nanoparticles capable of forming a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when atomic-size and electronegativity differences are within a range favorable to single-phase solid-solution formation.
The mechanism may not apply outside the stated compositional and processing limits.
Prior studies support the proposed qualitative stability trend.
The magnitude of stability improvement depends on the specific element combination.
Failure of reduced-entropy nanoparticles to show significantly greater segregation or chemical heterogeneity than high-entropy nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
